extraction.name: OpenThoughts3-1.2M
extraction.description: An open-source supervised fine-tuning (SFT) dataset for training reasoning models, containing 1.2 million examples across math (850K), code (250K), and science (100K) domains. The dataset consists of question-thinking tokens-answer triplets generated using QwQ-32B as a teacher model.
extraction.creator: Etash Guha, Ryan Marten, Sedrick Keh, Negin Raoof, Georgios Smyrnis, Hritik Bansal, Marianna Nezhurina, Jean Mercat, Trung Vu, Zayne Sprague, and others from Stanford University, University of Washington, BespokeLabs.ai, Toyota Research Institute, UC Berkeley, UT Austin, UCLA, and other institutions
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was created through a multi-stage pipeline involving question sourcing from various sources (fully synthetic, semi-synthetic, and non-synthetic), question filtering using LLM-based methods, deduplication, and generating multiple answers per question using teacher models. Questions were sourced from online forums, contests, chatbot interactions, existing datasets, and LLM generation. The pipeline involved filtering questions based on difficulty and response length, deduplicating questions using exact match or fuzzy matching, and generating 16× answers per question using teacher models like DeepSeek-R1 and QwQ-32B.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data sources included StackExchange (CodeGolf, Physics, Biology), OpenCodeReasoning, OpenMath-2-Math, NuminaMath-1.5, organic chemistry textbooks (PDFs), CommonCrawl, FineWeb, competitive coding questions, and various other existing datasets. The experiments covered 27 different question sources for code, 21 sources for math, and 14 sources for science.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Questions were sourced from math, code, and science domains, then filtered, deduplicated (exact match for math/science, none for code), randomly sampled, and annotated by generating 16 answers per question using teacher models (QwQ-32B for all domains). Various filtering strategies were tested including GPT verification, majority consensus, response length-based filtering, and fastText classifiers, but no filtering was ultimately applied as it did not improve performance.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Multiple answer filtering strategies were evaluated including GPT verification, majority consensus filtering, response-length-based filtering, fastText classifiers, and removing non-English answers. Performance was measured by training models on filtered datasets and evaluating on downstream benchmarks. Analysis showed that no filtering strategy outperformed using all samples without filtering.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Teacher models: QwQ-32B (primary for all domains), DeepSeek-R1, Phi-4-Reasoning-Plus-14B, Claude 3.7 (with thinking mode). Additional tools: fastText classifier for code filtering (trained on CodeForces with DeepSeek-R1 positives and GPT-4o-mini negatives), GPT for verification experiments.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The work has several limitations including not exploring datasets for reinforcement learning, not exploring staged SFT or curriculum learning, and uncertainty about cross-domain transfer when domains are mixed. Open questions remain about how scaling data impacts performance as student models approach teacher performance, and how question-answer diversity interactions behave across different domains, dataset sizes, and model scales.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The project aims to enhance reasoning capabilities of open-source models while ensuring models refuse to respond to unsafe requests and comply with benign requests. Safety capabilities are evaluated to address potential social impacts.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of reasoning models in math, code, and science domains. The OpenThoughts3-1.2M dataset is used to train reasoning models that can output long chains of thought during inference time.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: All datasets and models are released and available on openthoughts.ai for community use.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Multiple answer generation per question (1×, 4×, 16× sampling), deduplication (exact match for math/science, no deduplication for code), random sampling of questions, and dataset mixing with domain-specific ratios (850,000 math, 250,000 code, 100,000 science datapoints)
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Question filtering using difficulty-based filtering (GPT-4o-mini for code) and response length filtering (GPT-4.1-mini for math/science), decontamination against evaluation sets using Indel similarity (75% threshold) and N-gram matching (N=13), and removal of contaminated samples

rai:dataCollection.evidence: Our full dataset begins with sourcing many questions in math, code, and science domains. The next step is filtering those questions, deduplicating the math and science questions, randomly sampling questions, and then generating multiple answers for each question. Our final dataset contains 1.2 million datapoints.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: We can broadly categorize our question sourcing techniques into three types: (1) Fully synthetic – an existing LLM generates questions with little-to-no seed material... (2) Semi-synthetic – an LLM uses existing data sources such as CommonCrawl or FineWeb (Penedo et al., 2024a) as seeds to form questions... (3) Non-synthetic – humans write the questions. Examples include StackExchange and ShareGPTCode. These questions often arise from online forums, contests, chatbot interactions, and other sources.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: Our experiments cover 27 different question sources for code questions, 21 sources for math, and 14 sources for science... For code, CodeGolf questions from StackExchange and competitive coding questions from OpenCodeReasoning (Ahmad et al., 2025) perform well... For math, both LLM-generated questions in openmath-2-math (Toshniwal et al., 2024) and human-written questions in NuminaMath (LI et al., 2024) score the highest... for science, the highest-scoring question generation strategies are physics questions from StackExchange and LLM-extracted questions from organic chemistry textbooks

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: This work has several limitations. We did not explore datasets for reinforcement learning, a standard training regime for building reasoning models. Within the SFT realm, we did not explore the use of staged SFT or curriculum learning to further improve performance... In each step of our pipeline, we selected strategies that maximized overall average benchmark performance, rather than optimizing for each domain individually. This choice assumes some level of cross-domain transfer; for instance, training on math data improves science performance. However, it's unclear whether such transfer persists once domains are mixed.
